interest: This file provides valuable insight into the commercial and political dilemmas surrounding the revival of Japanese foreign trade under the Allied Occupation in 1949. It highlights the stark contrast between the commercial acceptance of West German goods in the United States and the strong protectionist anxieties of U.S. domestic industries toward Japanese imports prior to the full absorption of the unitary exchange rate under the Dodge Line. Furthermore, it reveals the intense inter-city rivalry between devastated port cities like Yokohama and Kobe as municipal governments attempted to use grand trade expositions to lure foreign buyers and tourists, despite candid consular reports acknowledging that the 1949 Yokohama fair was considered a 'dismal failure.' Notably, the consular documentation also includes early diplomatic drafting work by Edward G. Seidensticker, Jr., who would go on to become one of America's foremost translators and scholars of Japanese literature.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.607) documents efforts and debates concerning the organization of trade fairs and industrial expositions in post-World War II occupied Japan during 1949. The correspondence encompasses inter-agency deliberations between the Department of State and the Department of the Army regarding a proposal to hold a Japanese trade exposition in the United States modeled on a successful German trade fair in New York, which SCAP and the Army advised against due to exchange rate adjustments and domestic American industry sensitivity. It also contains consular reporting from Kobe concerning municipal and prefectural initiatives to stage the 1950 Japan Trade and Industry Exposition, as well as a despatch from Tokyo enclosing an elaborate promotional pamphlet and tourist brochure for the March-June 1949 Japan Foreign Trade Fair in Yokohama, designed to promote Japanese export manufactures, foreign technological exhibits, and international tourism under SCAP auspices.

subfiles.about: Deputy to the Assistant Secretary of the Army Robert R. West relays SCAP's view that holding a Japanese trade fair in the United States should be deferred in favor of direct commercial representation abroad.
subfiles.from: Robert R. West, Deputy to Assistant Secretary of the Army
subfiles.summary: Robert R. West responds to W. Walton Butterworth's inquiry concerning the feasibility of organizing a Japanese trade fair in the United States, transmitting SCAP's assessment that the timing is unpropitious. SCAP concluded that fair benefits were intangible and that promotional funds would be better directed toward sending Japanese commercial agents abroad to directly engage overseas markets. West concurs, adding that organizing a fair in the U.S. would trigger substantial domestic industrial criticism until the effects of the new unitary exchange rate and the removal of export subsidies stabilize landed import costs.
subfiles.title: Letter from Robert R. West to W. Walton Butterworth Regarding Proposed Japanese Trade Fair in the United States
subfiles.to: W. Walton Butterworth, Director for Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Director for Far Eastern Affairs W. Walton Butterworth asks the Department of the Army to consider holding a Japanese trade fair in the United States following the success of the German Trade Fair in New York.
subfiles.from: W. Walton Butterworth, Director for Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: W. Walton Butterworth writes to Robert R. West noting that the recently held German Trade Fair in New York had proved a significant success, generating over $30 million in firm merchandise orders with minimal public opposition. In light of this, Butterworth asks whether the Department of the Army has considered sponsoring a comparable trade fair for Japanese goods in the United States. He requests West's thoughts and perspective on the potential viability of such an undertaking.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. Walton Butterworth to Robert R. West Inquiring About a Japanese Trade Fair in the United States
subfiles.to: Robert R. West, Deputy to Assistant Secretary of the Army, Department of the Army

subfiles.about: Consul Douglas Jenkins, Jr. reports on plans developed by local municipal and prefectural authorities to stage the Japan Trade and Industry Exposition in Kobe in 1950.
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, Jr., American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Douglas Jenkins, Jr. informs the Secretary of State about meetings with officials from the Hyogo Prefectural Government, Kobe Municipal Government, and Kobe Chamber of Commerce and Industry regarding plans for the Japan Trade and Industry Exposition scheduled for March 15 to June 15, 1950. Budgeted at approximately 471.8 million yen ($1.31 million), the exposition was spearheaded by the Kobe Municipal Government to restore Kobe as a preeminent hub of Japanese international commerce. Jenkins cautions that the proposal is in an embryonic stage and faces steep challenges in attracting foreign buyers away from Tokyo, noting that a similar exposition recently held in Yokohama was considered a dismal failure.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 125 from Douglas Jenkins, Jr., on Plans to Hold Japan Trade and Industry Exposition in Kobe

subfiles.about: The U.S. Acting Political Adviser in Tokyo transmits promotional materials for the Yokohama Foreign Trade Fair and conveys requests for American exhibits and publicity.
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser, Tokyo (drafted by Edward G. Seidensticker, Jr.)
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser forwards fifteen copies of an advertising pamphlet and poster for the Yokohama Foreign Trade Fair scheduled to run from March 15 to June 15, 1949. Kanagawa Prefectural officials expressed difficulty in procuring materials for the Foreign Countries Pavilion and requested favorable publicity in the United States, emphasizing their desire to exhibit modern American ceramics and glassware. The despatch also details shipping arrangements, noting that exhibitors bear transit costs to Yokohama, whereas the fair committee covers local transit from dockside to the exposition site.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 56 from Acting Political Adviser on Yokohama Foreign Trade Fair

subfiles.about: An official English-language illustrated promotional brochure outlining pavilion exhibits, leadership, regulations, and regional tourism for the 1949 Japan Foreign Trade Fair in Yokohama.
subfiles.from: The Japan Foreign Trade Fair / Kanagawa Prefectural Government and Yokohama City
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive promotional brochure details the program, governance, pavilion structure, and tourist attractions associated with the Japan Foreign Trade Fair 1949, held in Yokohama from March 15 to June 15, 1949. Organized jointly by Kanagawa Prefecture and Yokohama City with SCAP authorization, the fair featured specialized pavilions for foreign trade merchandise, domestic manufacturing, scientific inventions, prefectural specialties, children's welfare, and foreign country advancements including atomic power and plastics. Integrated within the industrial prospectus are advertisements and itineraries prepared by the Japan Travel Bureau and premier resort hotels in the Fuji-Hakone region to entice international business buyers and tourists.
subfiles.title: Pamphlet and Guide to the Japan Foreign Trade Fair 1949 in Yokohama
subfiles.to: Foreign commercial buyers, exhibitors, and international visitors
